identificationTraits: Long, pointed snout — the basis for the common name, and generally longer/more slender than the snouts of small Carcharhinus species such as blacknose or finetooth shark.

Adults show white spots scattered on the back and sides, plus pale edges on the pectoral fins — a mark NOAA's tagging-program guide specifically uses to separate Atlantic sharpnose from finetooth shark, which lacks the white spotting.
Second dorsal fin originates over or behind the middle of the anal fin (NOAA tagging-program ID guide, given in the finetooth-shark comparison).
Juveniles show black edging on the dorsal and caudal fin margins, which is not present, or much reduced, in adults.
24-25 rows of small triangular teeth in each jaw (NOAA species overview) — a lab/hand-examination feature, not a field mark for a fish still in the water.
identification.coloration: Gray to gray-brown above in several shades, white below; adults have white spots on the sides and pale pectoral-fin margins; juveniles have black-edged dorsal and caudal fins.
identification.juvenileAppearance: Black-edged dorsal and caudal fins, which fade toward the adult white-spotted pattern with growth (NOAA species overview).
identification.adultAppearance: A small gray shark with a long pointed snout, scattered white spots on the back and sides, and pale-edged pectoral fins.

similarSpecies.name: Finetooth shark (Carcharhinus isodon)
similarSpecies.distinction: NOAA's tagging-program guide draws this comparison directly: Atlantic sharpnose has white spots on the back and sides and a second dorsal fin over or behind the middle of the anal fin; finetooth lacks the white spotting.

similarSpecies.name: Blacknose shark (Carcharhinus acronotus)
similarSpecies.distinction: Both are small, open-for-harvest requiem sharks placed in FWC's no-minimum Group 1, so the regulatory stakes of confusing them are low, but they are frequently caught together inshore. A dedicated field-mark comparison was not found in the sources reviewed this session; recorded as a gap rather than invented.

similarSpecies.name: Caribbean sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon porrosus)
similarSpecies.distinction: A close congener with a similar long-snouted body plan; the two are best separated in southern Gulf/Caribbean waters where ranges overlap. A specific field-mark comparison was not found in the sources reviewed this session; recorded as a gap.

similarSpecies.name: Juvenile blacktip or spinner shark
similarSpecies.distinction: Small juvenile blacktip/spinner can be superficially similar in size and general shape to an adult sharpnose; the long, sharply pointed sharpnose snout and its white side-spotting are the clearest quick separators from the rounder-snouted, black-fin-tipped blacktip/spinner juveniles.

identification.averageAdultLength: NOAA's species page gives two figures for maximum size that do not agree with each other: the page's running text states 'up to 32 inches,' while its quick-facts summary states 'up to 4 feet' (48 in). This internal disagreement is recorded here rather than resolved by picking one.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Females mature around 24 in (Atlantic stock, ~age 2) or 25 in (Gulf stock, ~age 1.3 years) per NOAA; most inshore recreational catches are mature or near-mature fish in this size range.
identification.typicalWeight: Not found in an agency source reviewed this session; recorded as a gap.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: See averageAdultLength — NOAA's own page gives conflicting maximum-length figures (32 in vs. 4 ft) that this record does not resolve.

social.note: Described in NOAA sources as common and abundant inshore, consistent with loose aggregation rather than solitary habits, though a dedicated schooling-behavior account was not found.

feedingStrategy.note: NOAA describes a diet of small fish (menhaden, eels, silversides, wrasses) taken by pursuit, plus invertebrates (worms, shrimp, crabs, mollusks) that imply some benthic foraging as well.

dielTendency.note: Not resolved to a specific diel pattern from a sourced account this session; recorded as a gap.

behavior.seasonalActivity: NOAA describes a seasonal inshore/offshore migration: this species moves to deeper offshore water in winter and returns to inshore water in spring to mate and give birth.
behavior.currentFacing: Not resolved from a sourced account; recorded as a gap.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Annual mating mid-May through mid-July in inshore waters; 10-11 month gestation; about four pups per litter delivered in nearshore areas each June. Recorded as conservation context only.

seasonal_calendar.overview: A small, abundant inshore/nearshore requiem shark that NOAA describes as moving offshore into deeper water in winter and returning inshore in spring to mate and pup in bays, estuaries, and surf-zone habitat over mud and sand.

entries.habitatClass: Deeper offshore water, per NOAA's described seasonal migration.
entries.movementTendency: Moves out of inshore bays/estuaries/surf zones into deeper water offshore.
entries.presentationImplication: Nearshore bottom-contact fishing is the reviewed family that best fits a winter offshore posture within the water types this catalog covers; no offshore-specific presentation is claimed here.
invalidators: fishing inshore flats/creeks for this species in winter on the assumption it behaves the same as in spring/summer

entries.habitatClass: Returns to inshore bays, estuaries, and surf-zone habitat over mud and sand to mate.
entries.presentationImplication: Tidal drift bait and live/natural bait suspension in bays and creek mouths, plus surf bait soak in the surf zone, are the reviewed families that fit a small bottom/mid-water opportunistic feeder returning inshore.
entries.conservationNote: Spring mating is biology, not a targeting cue.
invalidators: treating the spring return as a predictable bite window
